headline: iPhone prices set to rise due to soaring RAM costs
summary: Soaring memory costs are driving up prices across the tech industry, with no end to the crunch in sight. This "chipflation" is reversing decades of declining memory prices.
details: When Apple debuts the next generation of iPhones, they are likely to come with an unwanted change: a higher price tag. A price hike from the supply-chain powerhouse would be the clearest sign yet that soaring memory costs have become unavoidable.

This phenomenon, dubbed "chipflation" or "RAMageddon," is reversing a decades-long decline in memory costs that helped make consumer electronics more powerful without making them dramatically more expensive. The terms "memory prices" and "memory shortage" appeared in 473 company transcripts last quarter.

While generative AI is often blamed for driving up costs, the memory shortage was brewing well before ChatGPT took off. The current market is the product of a complicated reshuffling within the memory industry, which was already failing to keep up with demand.

Manufacturers like Micron have stated that they need to build more wafer capacity, a challenge different from previous years where technology alone could meet demand. Technological advances alone are no longer creating enough capacity to keep pace with long-term demand.

The memory business is also extraordinarily concentrated, with three manufacturers (Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron) accounting for about 90 percent of the market. This leaves the world dependent on a handful of companies to divide limited capacity between AI infrastructure and consumer devices.

The memory inside your phone or computer broadly falls into two buckets: DRAM, which temporarily holds information, and NAND flash memory for longer-term storage. Inside AI data centers, specialized processors rely heavily on a form of DRAM called high-bandwidth memory (HBM).

headline_marked: [[GTA Vice City & III]] return to browsers via open-source reverse engineering
headline: GTA Vice City & III return to browsers via open-source reverse engineering
summary: Classic Grand Theft Auto titles are now playable in web browsers, achieving over 100 FPS performance thanks to community-driven decompilation projects.
details: Grand Theft Auto: Vice City and Grand Theft Auto III have been made playable in web browsers, years after their original releases. The projects, hosted on a site called "Quenq," leverage community-driven reverse engineering efforts.

The Vice City port is built using reVC, a project that decompiles the game's source code into C++. This code is then translated into JavaScript via WebAssembly and rendered using WebGL 2, allowing it to run natively in a browser.

This browser port supports keyboard, mouse, and controller inputs, as well as touchscreen controls. It also includes a save game and mod manager, and allows for the use of external keyboards to input cheat codes.

While the original game was designed for 30 FPS, this port supports unlocked framerates, with users reporting performance exceeding 100 FPS on desktop systems. An FPS limit option is available to prevent potential physics bugs.
GTA III is also available on the same platform, likely built using re3, the decompiled source code for that title. It shares similar features to the Vice City port, though it omits the mod manager.
Previously, these browser ports were available on DOS Zone but were removed due to a DMCA takedown notice from Take-Two. The new platform appears to have shifted its distribution methods in response.
